items.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025
items.q: Your friend and sometimes bandmate Alan Broadbent described that when you bring in an arrangement and you hear it for the first time, he called it the “cringe moment.”

ctx.x: No, they handled the melody. They wanted me to keep time. So I locked in with the gut bucket player and – this was an upright piano with thumbtacks in the hammers to get that old barroom Western piano effect. And the two banjo players, father and son, were sitting up on top of the piano so I’m looking at their feet on the left and the right of me. And as I remember I just kept time and I did some rudimentary improvising. I was – I didn’t – I don’t know how they got my name and I don't know why they called me…

There’s a lot to be said for that, develop your own style. I think the things you learn to do and not to do really make a strong impression on you when you’re trying it on your own. Your friend and sometimes bandmate Alan Broadbent described that when you bring in an arrangement and you hear it for the first time, he called it the “cringe moment.”

Also the joy moment. It’s so great to – especially if you’re working with a big band or orchestra like Alan does a lot and I do from time to time. It’s such a joy to hear it with live instruments. Now we can mock it up on synthesizers and before, in the old days, we couldn’t. We just played and heard it on the piano. But it’s the cringe moment but also joyous when it all comes together and it works. And you know it’s great, we had workshops back in the day, I remember I was a member of the BMI Writers Workshop in…
